summary.title: The Great Confusion About URIs
summary.one_liner: URI is the general term, URL and URN are subsets of it, and many language URI/URL parsing libraries are misnamed relative to the IETF terminology.
takeaways: URI is the superset term; every URL and URN is also a URI, but not the reverse.
A URL identifies a resource by its network location, while a URN names a resource without giving its location.
The IETF now prefers 'URI' and treats 'URL' as an informal concept, per RFC 3986 and RFC 3305.
Many standard library parsers (Python urllib.parse, Java java.net.URL, JavaScript URL, Go net/url) are named after URL, and their names don't always match their capabilities.
General-purpose URI parsers can extract scheme and path from non-protocol URIs such as mailto:, but cannot parse the path further because it depends on the scheme.
summary.summary: The author explains why the terms URI, URL and URN are used interchangeably, despite having distinct meanings defined by the IETF and RFCs. He gives definitions and examples for each, showing that URI is the general category, URL adds a network location, and URN names a resource without a location. He then ports a short Python parsing script to several languages and compares how each library handles different schemes and whether its naming follows IETF terminology. The post concludes that programmers should use URI when possible and check what their parsing tools actually do.
